title: The Covenant and the Greatest Commandment

date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: "Now therefore hearken, O Israel, unto the statutes and unto the judgments... Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it" (Deut 4:1–2).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:1–2, read in full (BibleHub).

claims.claim: "Your eyes have seen what the LORD did because of Baalpeor: for all the men that followed Baalpeor, the LORD thy God hath destroyed them from among you. But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day" (Deut 4:3–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:3–4, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:3–4 (read in full: the pestilence and sword overtook only the guilty).

claims.claim: The statutes and judgments are Israel's wisdom and understanding before the nations: "what nation is there so great, that hath statutes and judgments so righteous as all this law?" (Deut 4:5–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:5–8, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:5–6 (read in full).

claims.claim: "Take heed to thyself... teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons; specially the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb" (Deut 4:9–10).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:9–10, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:10 (read in full).

claims.claim: The theophany retold: the mountain burned with fire unto the midst of heaven, with darkness, clouds, and thick darkness; the voice of the words was heard, no similitude seen; the covenant declared — ten commandments on two tables of stone (Deut 4:11–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:11–14, read in full.

claims.claim: Because no similitude was seen, no graven image of any figure (male or female, beast, fowl, creeping thing, fish) may be made, and the sun, moon, stars and host of heaven — "which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven" — may not be worshipped (Deut 4:15–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:15–19, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:16–19 (read in full: the Canaanite, Egyptian and Zabian idolatries).

claims.claim: Egypt is "the iron furnace" from which the LORD took Israel "to be unto him a people of inheritance" (Deut 4:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:20, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:20 (read in full: a smelting furnace).

claims.claim: "The LORD was angry with me for your sakes, and sware that I should not go over Jordan... but I must die in this land" (Deut 4:21–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:21–22, read in full.

claims.claim: "Take heed unto yourselves, lest ye forget the covenant... For the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God" (Deut 4:23–24).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:23–24, read in full.

claims.claim: After remaining long in the land and corrupting themselves, Israel will be scattered among the nations and serve gods of wood and stone, "which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" — heaven and earth called to witness (Deut 4:25–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:25–28, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:26, 4:28 (read in full).

claims.claim: "But if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul... in the latter days, if thou turn to the LORD thy God... (for the LORD thy God is a merciful God;) he will not forsake thee, neither destroy thee, nor forget the covenant of thy fathers" (Deut 4:29–31). JFB's reading of "latter days" (the close of the captivities, or the age of the Messiah) is Traditional.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:29–31, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:30 (read in full). The text is Established; the "latter days" reading is Traditional, recorded as JFB's.

claims.claim: The theophany's uniqueness: no people heard the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire and lived; no god assayed to take a nation from the midst of another nation "by temptations, by signs, and by wonders, and by war"; "the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him" (Deut 4:32–35).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:32–35, read in full.

claims.claim: "Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart, that the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else" (Deut 4:36–39).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:36–39, read in full.

claims.claim: "Thou shalt keep therefore his statutes, and his commandments... that it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days upon the earth... for ever" (Deut 4:40).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:40, read in full.

claims.claim: Three cities of refuge east of Jordan: Bezer in the plain country, of the Reubenites; Ramoth in Gilead, of the Gadites; Golan in Bashan, of the Manassites — for the slayer who kills his neighbour unawares (Deut 4:41–43).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:41–43, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:41–43 (read in full).

claims.claim: "And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel" — in the valley over against Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon and of Og king of Bashan, from Aroer by the Arnon even unto Mount Sion (Hermon), and all the plain eastward even unto the sea of the plain, under the springs of Pisgah (Deut 4:44–49).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:44–49, read in full; JFB on Deut 4:46, 4:49 (read in full: Beth-peor, Ashdoth-pisgah).

claims.claim: Horeb is the mountain of Deut 4:10–15 and 5:2; Exodus names the same mountain Sinai. The two names denote the same theophany mountain in the two books' usage.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 4:10, 15; 5:2 and Ex 19–20, read in full; JFB on Deut 1:6 (shared record §6): "Horeb was the general name of a mountainous district... whereas Sinai was the name appropriated to a particular peak."

claims.claim: Horeb/Sinai: site identity Unknown; event correlation Unknown; no event pin (shared geography record §6).
claims.evidence: Shared record `verification/shared/historical-geography-deuteronomy.md` §6 (read in full); Hoffmeier/Kitchen via search excerpts only (shared record). Established as a negative fact — the location is not established.

claims.claim: No direct archaeological evidence for the Horeb theophany as narrated.
claims.evidence: Exodus covenant dossier §6.2, clm-co-079 (prior Gnosis research, reused via the shared record §6). The absence is established; it is not filled with a reconstruction.

claims.claim: "The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. The LORD made not this covenant with our fathers, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day" (Deut 5:1–3). K&D's reading — "fathers" are the patriarchs; the covenant was made with the nation as an organic whole, not with particular individuals — is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:1–3, read in full (text Established); K&D on Deut 5 (read in part: vv. 1–5). The K&D reading is a commentary judgment, capped at Probable.

claims.claim: "The LORD talked with you face to face in the mount out of the midst of the fire, (I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to shew you the word of the LORD: for ye were afraid by reason of the fire...)" (Deut 5:4–5). JFB: "face to face — not in a visible and corporeal form... but freely, familiarly"; Moses as mediator is a type of Christ (Gal 3:19; 1 Tim 2:5; Heb 8:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:4–5, read in full (text Established); JFB on Deut 5:4–5 (read in full). The JFB readings are commentary judgments; the typology is Traditional.

claims.claim: The Decalogue in Deut 5:6–21 agrees in substance with Ex 20:1–17.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:6–21 and Ex 20:1–17, both read in full (BibleHub).

claims.claim: The wording differences between Deut 5:6–21 and Ex 20:1–17: "Remember" vs "Keep" (5:12 / Ex 20:8); the Sabbath rationale (see 024); the rest list particularised with ox, ass and "any of thy cattle" plus "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou" (5:14); "that it may go well with thee" added (5:16); the repeated "Neither" (5:17–21); the wife placed first and "his field" added, with two verbs ("desire", "covet") in the tenth commandment (5:21); "the waters beneath the earth" (5:8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:6–21 and Ex 20:1–17, both read in full; catalogue in §5.1.

claims.claim: The Sabbath rationale is the chief difference between the two Decalogues: creation in Ex 20:11 ("For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth...") against deliverance in Deut 5:15 ("remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt...").
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:11 and Deut 5:15, read in full.

claims.claim: JFB on the Sabbath: the addition of another motive "does not imply any necessary contrariety"; the deliverance motive is "peculiarly seasonable" and probably secures rest for the servants.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 5:14 (read in full). A commentary reading, capped at Probable.

claims.claim: Deut 5:16's "that it may go well with thee" is the form Paul quotes in Eph 6:2–3 ("Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise; That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth") — it matches Deut 5:16, not Ex 20:12.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:16 and Ex 20:12, read in full (BibleHub); Eph 6:2–3 wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings as rendered in search results — multiple concordant listings, but not an opened page (see §12.4). Capped at Probable on that basis.

claims.claim: "These words the LORD spake unto all your assembly in the mount out of the midst of the fire, of the cloud, and of the thick darkness, with a great voice: and he added no more. And he wrote them in two tables of stone" (Deut 5:22). JFB's inference — the pre-eminence of the ten, spoken directly by God while the rest of the law came through Moses — is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:22, read in full (text Established); JFB on Deut 5:22 (read in full). The inference is a commentary judgment.

claims.claim: The people's fear and mediation request parallels Ex 20:18–21 with expansion: the heads of the tribes and the elders come near; "we have seen this day that God doth talk with man, and he liveth"; "Go thou near, and hear all that the LORD our God shall say" (Deut 5:23–27).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:23–27 and Ex 20:18–21, both read in full; K&D on Deut 5 (read in part: vv. 24–27 as a rhetorical and more exact account of Ex 20:18–20).

claims.claim: God's approval: "They have well said all that they have spoken. O that there were such an heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always, that it might be well with them, and with their children for ever!" (Deut 5:28–29). Whether "O that" is anthropopathic language (a divine wish) is Debated; K&D's explanation (the words sprang from a consciousness of unworthiness, which God approved) is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:28–29, read in full (text Established); K&D on Deut 5 (read in part); JFB on Deut 5:29 (read in full: God can bestow such a heart, Jer 32:40).

claims.claim: "But as for thee, stand thou here by me, and I will speak unto thee all the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments, which thou shalt teach them... Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left" (Deut 5:30–33).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 5:30–33, read in full; K&D on Deut 5 (read in part: vv. 32–33).

claims.claim: "Not with our fathers" (Deut 5:3) admits three readings: not with the fathers only; not at all, if the Sinai ratification is meant; not with the fathers who died in the wilderness.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 5:3 (read in full, catalogues the three readings); K&D on Deut 5 (read in part: fathers = the patriarchs). No reading is adopted as settled.

claims.claim: The LXX of Deut 5 gives the commandments in the order murder, adultery, steal — the same as the MT — not the Adultery–Steal–Murder order of LXX Ex 20.
claims.evidence: Brenton LXX Deut 5:17–19, read in full via the ellopos bilingual page (Greek + English); Nash Papyrus article (read in full) confirms the Adultery–Murder–Steal order is that of "most texts of the Septuagint" for Exodus.

claims.claim: LXX Deut 5:12 φυλάξαι "Keep the day of the sabbaths"; 5:15 retains the deliverance rationale; 5:16 "that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest live long."
claims.evidence: NETS Deuteronomy (read in part: Deut 5:12–6:25 region); Brenton LXX Deut 5 (read in full via ellopos).

claims.claim: "Now these are the commandments, the statutes, and the judgments, which the LORD your God commanded to teach you, that ye might do them in the land whither ye go to possess it: that thou mightest fear the LORD thy God... and that thy days may be prolonged... in the land that floweth with milk and honey" (Deut 6:1–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:1–3, read in full.

claims.claim: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deut 6:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:4, read in full.

claims.claim: *šāmaʿ* (H8085) means hear with attention, understand, hear a judicial case, listen/give heed, obey — so the Shema's "Hear" is obedient hearing, not bare audition.
claims.evidence: BDB on H8085 *šāmaʿ* (read in part, BibleHub Strong's page; Qal senses listed; *bĕqôl* = obey, Deut 4:30 cited; Hiphil "cause to hear", Deut 4:10, 36 cited).

claims.claim: *ʾeḥād* (H259) is the numeral "one... properly united, i.e. one; (as an ordinal) first."
claims.evidence: BDB on H259 *ʾeḥād* (read in part, BibleHub Strong's page; senses 1–8, including "one and the same", "as one man, together", "only", "first").

claims.claim: The Shema's Hebrew (four nouns, no copula) admits several renderings — "YHWH our God, YHWH is one" / "YHWH is our God, YHWH alone" — and no single rendering is imposed by the grammar.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "The Shema" (read in full: the Hebrew wording is ambiguous); Clarke on Deut 6:4 (read in full: five renderings, "almost all possible verbal varieties... amount to the same sense").

claims.claim: The Shema's preexilic sense is covenant loyalty to YHWH alone (monolatry), with a monotheistic rereading in the Second Temple period (LXX "YHWH is one"; Nash Papyrus).
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "The Shema" (read in full). One scholarly reading; the counter-reading (Deut 4:35, 39 as exclusive monotheism) is the text's own confession (clm-deu-02-012, 013). See §8.1.

claims.claim: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (Deut 6:5). *mĕʾōd* (H3966) as a substantive means "might, force, abundance."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:5, read in full (verse text Established); Strong's H3966 gloss via the BibleHub interlinear listing (search-surfaced; BDB entry not opened — see §12.4).

claims.claim: Mark 12:29–30 quotes Deut 6:4 verbatim ("Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord") and adapts 6:5, adding "mind" and keeping "strength."
claims.evidence: KJV Mark 12:29–30 and Deut 6:4–5, read in full (BibleGateway page for Mark; BibleHub for Deut).

claims.claim: The "mind" addition in Mark 12:30 (and Matt 22:37; Luke 10:27) is explained by the LXX: NETS Deut 6:5 renders "with the whole of your mind and with the whole of your soul and with the whole of your power."
claims.evidence: NETS Deuteronomy 6:5 (read in part — wording Established); the inference that the Gospels follow the LXX form is a scholarly judgment, capped at Probable.

claims.claim: Matt 22:37 adapts rather than quotes: no Deut 6:4, and Deut 6:5 reduced to heart, soul, mind — "might"/strength dropped, "mind" added.
claims.evidence: KJV Matt 22:37 and Deut 6:4–5, read in full (BibleGateway page for Matt; BibleHub for Deut).

claims.claim: Luke 10:27 combines all four terms (heart, soul, strength, mind) and joins Lev 19:18 ("and thy neighbour as thyself"); spoken by the lawyer, affirmed by Jesus.
claims.evidence: KJV Luke 10:27 and Deut 6:5, read in full (BibleGateway page for Luke; BibleHub for Deut).

claims.claim: "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates" (Deut 6:6–9). Clarke's gloss on *šinnantām* ("repeat, iterate, whet, sharpen") is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:6–9, read in full (text Established); Clarke on Deut 6:7 (read in full: *shinnantam* from *shanan*, to repeat/iterate, to whet/sharpen).

claims.claim: The historic Jewish reading of Deut 6:8–9 is literal — tefillin (four passages: Ex 13:2–10, 13:11–16; Deut 6:1–8; 11:18–21) and mezuzah, attested from antiquity to the present. Whether Moses intended the language figuratively (JFB: "probable... merely in a figurative way") is Debated.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 6:7–8 (read in full: the tefillin form described); Josephus, *Antiquities* 4.8.13 (read in part); Bible Odyssey, "The Shema" (read in full: mezuzah custom "from antiquity to the present day"). The practice is Traditional; the intent is Debated.

claims.claim: The Nash Papyrus (Cambridge UL, MS Or.233): 24 lines, the Ten Commandments and the start of the Shema (Deut 6:4–5), blending Ex 20 and Deut 5, omitting "house of bondage," in parts closer to the LXX than the MT; order Adultery–Murder–Steal; dated c. 150–100 BCE (Albright; Cook first dated 2nd century CE); the oldest known Hebrew biblical manuscript before the Dead Sea Scrolls (1947); likely a liturgical or phylactery document.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, "Nash Papyrus" (read in full). Cook 1903 and Albright 1937 were not read directly — the facts rest on the secondary article, capped at Probable (see §12.4).

claims.claim: The Nash Papyrus's preamble before the Shema (taken from Deut 4:45) also stands in the LXX before Deut 6:4.
claims.evidence: Nash Papyrus article (read in full); NETS Deuteronomy (read in part: the preamble interpolation before 6:4).

claims.claim: "When thou shalt have eaten and be full; then beware lest thou forget the LORD... Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name. Ye shall not go after other gods... (for the LORD thy God is a jealous God among you)" (Deut 6:10–15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:10–15, read in full; Clarke on Deut 6:12 (read in full: prosperity breeds forgetfulness).

claims.claim: Deut 6:13, "Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name": Clarke's textual note — the LXX, Vulgate, Coptic and Anglo-Saxon preserve "him only shalt thou serve" (αὐτῷ μόνῳ; לְבַדּוֹ), absent from the printed Hebrew text and all MSS discovered (Kennicott).
claims.evidence: Clarke on Deut 6:13 (read in full). The LXX Greek of Deut 6:13 was not opened in this session; the Matt 4:10 / Luke 4:8 wordings confirm the form's currency (see §5.4).

claims.claim: "Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah" (Deut 6:16). The Massah identification with Ex 17:1–7 ("Is the LORD among us, or not?") is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:16, read in full (verse text Established); Clarke on Deut 6:16 (read in full: Massah, Ex 17:1–7).

claims.claim: "Ye shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies, and his statutes... And thou shalt do that which is right and good in the sight of the LORD: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest go in and possess the good land... to cast out all thine enemies from before thee" (Deut 6:17–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:17–19, read in full.

claims.claim: The son's question and the exodus answer: "We were Pharaoh's bondmen in Egypt; and the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand... And it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments before the LORD our God, as he hath commanded us" (Deut 6:20–25). Clarke's reading of "righteousness" as evidence of the fear and love of God, not the purchase of heaven, is Probable.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:20–25, read in full (text Established); Clarke on Deut 6:25 (read in full).

claims.claim: Deut 6:25, "it shall be our righteousness" (KJV/MT), against the LXX "there will also be mercy for us" (NETS) — a genuine variant in the transmission.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 6:25 and NETS Deut 6:25, both read directly (BibleHub; NETS PDF, read in part).

claims.claim: The covenant as presented in Deut 4–6 is conditional in form: blessing for obedience, exile for breach, restoration on repentance.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "Covenant in the Hebrew Bible" (read in full: the conditional vs eternal covenant; Deut 28–30; Lev 26; Jer 31:31–34); KJV Deut 4:25–31, read in full.

claims.claim: The absolute date of the speeches in Deut 4–6 is not given in the text and is not established by any source read for this dossier.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 1:3 (the fortieth year, read in full); no dating source was read directly in this session. The traditional Mosaic dating (c. 1406 BCE) and the modern critical dating (7th–5th centuries BCE) are recorded in clm-deu-01-025 (Debated).

connections.note: The Horeb theophany retold: the mountain burning, the voice, the ten commandments. Deut 4 retells Ex 19 as memory and argument.
"Ten commandments... two tables of stone" — the covenant's terms in both accounts.
Baal-peor: the event Deut 4:3–4 draws its warning from.
The cities of refuge: the institution Deut 4:41–43 names.
The same institution: the six cities appointed, three east of Jordan.
The fuller refuge law (Category 5): the three eastern cities completed by three western ones.
The parallel Decalogue: same substance, wording differences (§5.1).
The two tables of stone "written with the finger of God."
The people's fear and mediation request: the parallel account, expanded in Deut 5.

"Ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire" — the terrifying mountain (the Hebrews text was not re-opened in this session; the parallel is the BibleHub cross-reference on Ex 20:18–21, read in full).
Paul quotes the fifth commandment in the Deut form: "that it may be well with thee" (Deut 5:16, not Ex 20:12). Wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings.
Quotation of 6:4 verbatim + adaptation of 6:5 ("mind" added, "strength" kept). Wordings read in full (BibleGateway).
Adaptation, not quotation: no 6:4; 6:5 reduced to heart, soul, mind. Wording read in full (BibleGateway).
Adaptation/combination: all four terms, joined to Lev 19:18; spoken by the lawyer, affirmed by Jesus. Wording read in full (BibleGateway).

"There is none other God but one... But to us there is but one God, the Father... and one Lord Jesus Christ" — Paul's monotheism confession echoes the Shema; not a quotation. Wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings.
The second Shema paragraph (Category 3): the love-command and the bind/write language restated.
"It shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes" — the shared sign formula.
"It shall be for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes" — the same formula, for the firstborn.
"They make broad their phylacteries" — Jesus on the literal observance of Deut 6:8.
"Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve" — the *lebaddo* form (see §8.7). Wording verified via BibleGateway/search-rendered KJV text.
The same words in Luke's temptation account. Wording verified via BibleGateway (Luke 4:1–13, KJV).
Massah: "Is the LORD among us, or not?" — the testing Deut 6:16 names.
"Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness" — the Massah/Meribah memory.
Hebrews quotes Ps 95:7–11 on the same testing.
The son's question about the Passover: "What mean ye by this service?" — the parallel catechetical form.
The son's question about the firstborn: "What is this?" — "By strength of hand the LORD brought us out from Egypt."
"When your children shall ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean these stones?" — the same catechetical form for the memorial stones.
"Ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart" — the seek-and-find promise taken up in the exilic letter.
"I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me" — the "none else" confession in the prophets.
"For our God is a consuming fire" — the exact phrase. Wording verified via BibleGateway/search-rendered KJV text.
"Ye shall not add... neither shall ye diminish" beside "If any man shall add unto these things... if any man shall take away" — the same formula, not a quotation.
"I will give them one heart... that they shall not depart from me" — JFB cites Jer 32:40 on Deut 5:29 (God bestowing the heart).
"I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day" — the same covenant-witness formula (Category 8).
"In that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one" — the Shema's oneness in the eschatological promise.
"What doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God... and to love him... with all thy heart and with all thy soul" (Category 3).
"The LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart... to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul" (Category 8).
"The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul... The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart" — the law as wisdom.

Paul's list ("Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet") follows the LXX order — adultery first. Wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings.
"He that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill" — the same LXX order. Wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings.
"Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery..." — murder first, the MT order. Wording verified via BibleGateway KJV listings.
The host of heaven "divided unto all nations" beside "when the most High divided to the nations their inheritance... For the LORD's portion is his people" (Category 9).
"Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands... They that make them are like unto them" — gods of wood and stone that neither see nor hear.
"For thou art a gracious and merciful God" — the merciful God who does not forsake, in the post-exilic confession.
"A peculiar treasure unto me above all people" — the people of inheritance.
"It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Wording verified via search-rendered KJV text (wordofgodtoday.org, citing Deut 6:16).
"It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Wording verified via BibleGateway (Luke 4:1–13, KJV).
